OPENcverify,thuman,eenergy,nreset).\displaystyle c_{\mathrm{verify}},t_{\mathrm{human}},e_{\mathrm{energy}},n_{\mathrm{reset}}).

Transition counts, robot time, training and verification compute, human time, energy, and resets are not interchangeable. Match componentwise ceilings and report actual consumption. Candidate discovery, rejected updates, recovery, and maintenance belong in the end-to-end record. Report improver construction separately from recurring use, with explicit amortization assumptions. When exact matching is impossible, compare a prespecified budget grid and performance–resource frontier. Any scalar conversion needs stated rates and sensitivity analysis.

Separate development feedback from concealed reporting audits. Checkpoint scores that influence subsequent updates become development information for those later rounds, even if the underlying episodes remain hidden. Preserve a terminal holdout until the improvement procedure and analysis decisions are frozen. Version task generators, models, code, intervention records, and access permissions so that the evidence available to each updater can be reconstructed.

Uncertainty must follow the assignment structure. Episodes sharing a task, robot, site, or seed are not automatically independent replicates; analyze paired contrasts within blocks and use cluster-aware uncertainty where appropriate. Report old-skill changes against a fixed anchor alongside new-task gains, because acceptable average retention can conceal loss of an essential skill. Safety conclusions require an event definition, exposure, and interruption policy: zero observed incidents is not zero risk, and shielded trials evaluate the shield–learner combination. Intervention frequency is needed to interpret apparent safety and autonomy. Table V brings these requirements together, linking each comparison condition to the information needed to interpret an improver-gain claim.

VI-D Quantitative results for policies, memory, and system evolution

Quantitative results show how these mechanisms operate in different tasks. Manipulation policies are typically evaluated by success rate, while memory and harness methods additionally address partially observed state, long task sequences, and reuse across tasks. We compare LIBERO, EmbodiedBench, RoboMemArena, and RoboDojo separately and interpret gains using each study’s initial system and resource conditions. Benchmark scores describe the evaluated configuration; within-study before-and-after contrasts more directly show the change associated with an improvement.

EmbodiedBench supports several distinct improvement routes. RoboFoundry revises the executable agent during the evaluated stream, whereas EmbodiSkill develops reusable skills before held-out testing. MemCompiler trains state-dependent memory use, and ERA updates a compact policy through embodied prior learning and online reinforcement learning. Their reported scores locate these mechanisms within task benchmarks; the update boundary and training resources determine which comparisons isolate an improvement effect.[61, 58, 220, 221]

Memory-dependent manipulation involves both retained state and reliable execution. Table VI compares memory-augmented VLAs, WAM execution controls, HarnessWAM, and RoboFoundry on the full 26-task benchmark. HarnessWAM tests structured state maintenance and recovery during execution, linking task performance to how memory is used.

HyMeS evaluates a learned executable memory heuristic that is frozen at test time. On its selected 12-task evaluation (160 episodes), it reports overall TSR and CSR of 60.1% and 66.2%, compared with 45.6% and 61.7% for the re-evaluated PrediMem baseline. This within-study comparison uses corrected success checks and a selected task set, distinct from the full-benchmark results.[222]

LIBERO results show that policy gains can be obtained through different interfaces. RedFlow converts fixed failure experience into corrections, increasing average success from 56.2% to 68.2% in its setting. Q-Planning keeps the FastWAM action generator frozen and improves action selection, raising the four-suite mean from approximately 94.4% to 99.1% in its online setting. Q-VGM separates offline and online updates, while WoVR supports policy training with model-generated experience. These contrasts illustrate the roles of failure reuse, candidate evaluation, and imagined training. Different initial models and collection budgets explain why absolute scores or gain magnitudes cannot replace mechanism comparisons.[43, 44, 45, 50]

For system evolution, evaluation timing also affects interpretation. RoboFoundry’s streaming results include performance during adaptation, whereas a held-out test after freezing updates measures retained capability. The former describes improvement in operation; the latter describes the system obtained after improvement. [61]

Real-robot and system-level contrasts further connect gains to resources. FIND increases success from 55.0% to 71.9% across eight Franka tasks. LWD improves freezer restocking from 92.0% to 97.0% using online fleet experience. EmbodiRSI and RoboCoach change experience allocation, whereas RPG and SHAPER change reusable execution artifacts (Table IX). These results support capability improvement within different scopes. Retained trajectories, human demonstrations, fleet time, and test-time action limits describe different acquisition and execution costs; Table X gives the corresponding conditions.

RoboDojo supports both benchmark-wide submissions and studies of selected tasks. Table VII preserves a dated leaderboard snapshot: its category scores and terminal success rates summarize task performance. Table VIII shows why such results need a separate mechanism-level reading. HexaAnything and URAI examine tool revision with different forms of human participation; ENCORE evaluates discovered programs after development; RoboHarn-Evo transfers knowledge evolved on another benchmark. The action-model results of ME-Brain-1.0 assess a different part of its system. These protocols provide evidence about revision, transfer, or task competence, while a reusable improver advantage requires the controlled comparisons described above.[226, 227, 228, 106, 229]

VI-E Synthesis of the current evidence

The approaches establish multiple routes from experience to persistent capability: practice updates policies, prediction expands usable experience, skill libraries retain reusable behaviors, and harnesses organize their invocation. Revisions to rewards and training programs extend change to the process that produces capability. The common connection is that an interaction can influence later tasks and even the organization of later learning. Benchmarks and within-study contrasts reveal different parts of this relationship; improver comparisons from shared learner starts target the subsequent value of the process revision itself.

Digital-agent research contributes designs for this latter comparison. Dream-RSI and Escher-Loop evaluate programs that produce later solutions, while DGM analyzes system modification through related ablations. Together with robotic policy, memory, and harness results, these studies provide methodological references. Further development of physical RSI connects reusable process revisions to physical interaction budgets, recovery, and retention, testing whether their advantages accumulate during continued deployment. [69, 68, 35]

VII Open Challenges and Research Directions

When experience acquisition, feedback, and learning procedures can all be revised, sustained improvement also depends on their remaining compatible as they change together. The preceding comparisons direct attention to this continuity: feedback must remain grounded in physical outcomes, acquired capabilities and improvement procedures must survive further updates and transfer, and repeated experimentation requires reliable recovery at an affordable resource cost. Establishing progress also requires records of process versions, interventions, and evaluation conditions so that gains can be reproduced and attributed. The following research directions develop these connected requirements.

VII-A Grounded feedback that survives system change

The first priority is to maintain a reliable connection between internal feedback and physical outcomes as the system changes. Reward models need failure coverage, temporal context, calibration, and audits outside their training loop. Proposals such as intrinsic robot rewarding can contribute ideas, but proposed protocols must be distinguished from completed online experiments. A useful research target is not merely a higher reward-model score, but a feedback mechanism whose errors remain bounded under the distribution induced by continued improvement. [65, 144, 231]

VII-B Lasting gains and reusable improvers

A useful improvement should survive later updates and transfer beyond the failure that triggered it. This requires studying skill retirement, conflicting memories, representation drift, and compatibility between a revised improver and different learners. SkillSmith and Evo-Harness suggest ways to manage external artifacts, while morphology-design systems expose transfer across changing bodies. Physical studies should test whether a learned acquisition, verification, or update strategy benefits a new task or embodiment after its own development feedback is frozen. [232, 233, 66]

VII-C Recovery and resource-aware experimentation

Recovery should become part of the improvement objective rather than invisible laboratory labor. Systems need to reason about recoverable failure states, when to request assistance, and when an experiment should stop. Automated laboratories provide an adjacent physical setting in which experiments have delayed outcomes and material costs. They can inform provenance and scheduling, but successful automated synthesis does not itself establish an improving general-purpose robot or an improving research algorithm. [42, 168, 234]

Resource-aware search must include the cost of discovering the improver, not only the cost after discovery. Cheap simulated search may shift work to model construction, and fewer robot trials may require more demonstrations or human maintenance. Future benchmarks should expose these trade-offs as resource profiles rather than collapse them into one score. They should also include unsuccessful campaigns so that efficiency is not estimated only among survivors.

VII-D Reproducible process evidence and review limitations

Research should publish versioned learner and improver artifacts, acceptance decisions, intervention logs, and independent evaluation partitions. The verification gap in autonomous research and guidance-sensitive benchmarks such as ASI-Bench emphasize that finishing an experimental workflow, producing a plausible paper, and establishing a reproducible finding are different outcomes. Physical RSI needs the same distinction, augmented with hardware state and recovery records. [235, 236]

A concrete research target is an interchangeable improvement interface specifying inputs, editable components, admissible evidence, and resource limits. This would enable cross-learner tests without undocumented engineering changes. Cross-embodiment transfer should distinguish reuse of semantic knowledge, acquisition strategy, optimization code, and control representation; extensive human retuning changes the claim. Development evaluators may evolve, but the reporting outcome must retain a common interpretation. Changing success thresholds, task exclusions, or failure definitions can otherwise mimic progress without improving competence or improvement capacity.

The comparisons in this paper follow the retained artifacts, reset boundaries, and resource conditions reported for each evaluation protocol. Differences in task distributions, human assistance, and cost accounting limit direct comparisons across studies. The boundary between learner and improver follows a component’s actual role in subsequent updates. A shared annotation protocol and inter-rater agreement tests can further improve the reproducibility of comparisons using the L0–L3 rubric.

VIII Conclusion

Embodied self-improvement rests on turning interaction experience into capability that remains useful later. Policies, world models, memory, skills, and harnesses provide different routes for retaining and reusing that experience. Recursive self-improvement further changes how data are acquired, feedback is constructed, and updates are produced, allowing inherited process revisions to govern the next learning round. This relationship connects otherwise separate technical approaches while preserving their differences in supervision, update objects, and physical conditions.

This paper relates capability gains, process inheritance, and improver gains through the L0–L3 evidence rubric and compares their mechanisms and experimental results. Long-term progress in embodied RSI depends jointly on valid feedback, continued interaction, retention, and affordable improvement costs. Common-data and interactive comparisons of revised improvers can further distinguish a system that has acquired better task capability from one that has acquired a more effective process for developing capability.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
